analysis.one_liner: Ends every federal tax except Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes after 2000.
analysis.headline: The bill would have eliminated income, corporate, estate, gift, and excise taxes while keeping payroll taxes, but it never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have shut off every federal tax except the payroll taxes that fund Social Security and railroad retirement, starting after the year 2000. That means the federal income tax, corporate income tax, estate and gift taxes, and excise taxes would all end. The federal government would have lost most of its money — over $1 trillion a year at the time — while working households would have kept paying Social Security and Medicare taxes from every paycheck. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, high-income households and wealthy estates would have gained the most, because the taxes being eliminated — the income tax and the estate tax — are the ones that fall hardest on them. Meanwhile the payroll taxes the bill kept are flat taxes on wages that take a bigger share of a middle-class paycheck than a millionaire's income. Corporations would have stopped paying federal income tax entirely.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, wealthy estates, and corporations

how_it_helps.text: The bill ends all Internal Revenue Code taxes for years beginning after December 31, 2000, keeping only self-employment, Social Security (FICA), and railroad retirement payroll taxes [S2] [S3].

The taxes it keeps are flat payroll taxes on wages; the taxes it eliminates include the income tax, estate tax, gift tax, and excise taxes, which are the parts of the federal tax system that scale up with income and wealth [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would have lost the bulk of its revenue — everything funded by income, corporate, estate, and excise taxes, from defense and roads to interest on the national debt — forcing either massive spending cuts, huge new borrowing, or some replacement tax. Households earning wages would have kept paying the same payroll taxes, so the tax burden would have shifted away from wealth and toward work.

drawbacks.text: Ending income, corporate, estate, and excise taxes would remove most federal revenue, leaving the government unable to pay for existing programs without enormous cuts, new borrowing, or a replacement tax none of which the bill provides [S2] [S3].
Because the only taxes kept are flat payroll taxes on wages, the remaining tax system would take a larger share of income from ordinary wage earners than from high earners and wealth [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered the largest possible tax cut with no plan to replace the money or cut spending to match. Most households would have seen their income tax disappear, but they would have kept paying Social Security and Medicare taxes, and the loss of essentially all other federal revenue would have forced deep cuts to programs or a massive debt increase — costs that would fall back on the same households. The benefit to high-income households and wealthy estates would have been immediate and enormous; the cost to everyone else would have been delayed but far larger.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sam Brownback introduced the bill on September 29, 1997, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S1] [S5].
The Finance Committee took no further action; the bill's only other activity was the sponsor's introductory remarks, and it died when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained anything concrete, since the bill never advanced. The existing tax system stayed in place, which is worth more to ordinary wage earners than to high-income households and wealthy estates, who stood to gain most had it passed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; existing progressive tax code survived

for.name: Sen. Sam Brownback
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Republicans and no Democrat signed on, but the bill was too narrow in support to draw any recorded votes, so the partisan shape of the full chamber is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would have eliminated the income tax and estate tax, the parts of the federal system that fall most heavily on high incomes and large inheritances, while keeping flat payroll taxes on wages. Its gain would have come at the cost of the federal programs funded by those taxes.
Federal corporate income tax would have ended entirely, with no replacement revenue source specified in the bill.
